'''''Mammillaria vetula''''', the '''thimble cactus''', is a species of [[Mammillaria|nipple cactus]] in the subfamily [[Cactoideae]]. It is native to the [[Mexican states]] of [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]], [[Guanajuato]] and [[Querétaro]]. Two subspecies are recognized ''M. vetula'' subsp. '''''vetula''''' and ''M. vetula'' subsp. '''''gracilis'''''. While the former is usually considered too plain to be grown as an [[ornamental plant]], the latter is one of the most widespread mammillarias in cultivation.

==Taxonomy==
''Mammillaria vetula'' comprises two [[subspecies]], ''M. vetula'' subsp. ''vetula'' and ''M. vetula'' subsp. ''gracilis'', which were originally thought to be distinct species. ''M. kuentziana'' and ''M. magneticola'' are considered [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] of ''M. vetula'' subsp. ''vetula''.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> The [[specific epithet]] ''vetula'' means "little old one". The common name "thimble cactus" refers to the resemblance of the stems to little [[thimble]]s.<ref name="Extension">{{cite web | title=Mammillaria vetula (Thimble Cactus, Thimble mammillaria) | website=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox | url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/mammillaria-vetula/ | access-date=20 January 2025}}</ref>

==Description==
''Mammillaria vetula'' is a [[succulent]] [[subshrub]]<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=Plants of the World Online | website=Plants of the World Online | date=7 July 2019 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:151836-2 | access-date=20 January 2025}}</ref> which forms clusters of globose to short-cylindric, bluish-green stems with [[axil]]s that may be naked or slightly woolly.<ref name="Hunt">{{cite book | last1=Hunt | first1=David R.|author-link1=David Hunt (botanist) | last2=Taylor | first2=Nigel P. | last3=Charles | first3=G. | title=The New Cactus Lexicon | publisher=Dh Books | issue=v. 2 | year=2006 | isbn=978-0-9538134-6-9 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=up6vtQEACAAJ | access-date=17 January 2025 | page=178}}</ref><ref name="Extension"/> In ''M. vetula'' subsp. ''vetula'', young plants have 25 to 40 radial [[thorns, spines and prickles|spines]], increasing to 50 as they mature, and they remain white. Central spines number 1 or 2, but up to 5 to 9 have been observed in some specimens in [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]]. These spines are reddish-brown and about 10 mm long.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> The flowers are funnel-shaped,<ref name="Extension"/> [[lemon-yellow]], approximately 15 mm in length and width, with white (sometimes orange-yellow) [[stigma (botany)|stigmas]]. The fruit is dull pink, and the seeds are black.<ref name="Pilbeam"/>

''Mammillaria vetula'' subsp. ''gracilis'' is prolific, producing offsets that detach easily.<ref name="Hunt"/> Its stems are cylindrical, up to 13 cm long and 1 to 3 cm wide, with naked axils. It has 11 to 16 radial spines, 3 to 8 mm long, bristle-like, and chalky white (sometimes tipped brown in smaller variants). Central spines are absent or number up to 5 in mature plants, measuring 10 to 12 mm long and stronger than radials, either white or dark brown. The flowers are 12 mm long and wide, pale yellow with a pinkish or brownish midstripe. The fruit is small, red or pinkish-white, with black seeds.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> A form with smaller stems and brown spines also exists and is sometimes labeled ''M. fragilis'' or ''M. gracilis'' var. ''pulchella''; the botanist [[David Hunt (botanist)|David Hunt]] considers it a [[cultivar]].<ref name="Pilbeam"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Mammillaria vetula ssp vetula.jpg|thumb|''M. vetula'' subsp. ''vetula'' in its natural habitat, a rocky slope at about 1800 m [[above sea level]]]]
''Mammillaria vetula'' grows primarily in the [[desert]] and dry [[shrubland]].<ref name="POWO"/> ''M. mammillaria'' subsp. ''vetula'' is found in the [[Mexican states]] of [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]], [[Guanajuato]], and [[Querétaro]], at altitudes of 1,600 to 3,350 meters. At the highest altitudes it is often covered by snow and ice. Specific locations include [[San José del Oro]], [[La Encarnación]], [[Sierra de Jalapa]], and [[Vizarrón]]. ''M. vetula'' subsp. ''gracilis'' is known from Hidalgo and Querétaro, occurring at altitudes of 1,200 to 1,850 meters. Locations include [[Puente de Dios]], [[San Onofre, Ciudad Fernández|San Onofre]], [[Tolantongo]], [[Barranca Xilitla]], [[San Pedro Gilo]], [[Ixmiquilpan]], [[Metztitlan]].<ref name="Pilbeam"/> The type specimen was collected in leaf litter under shrubs on [[limestone]] rocks.<ref name="Hunt"/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Mammillaria gracilis cv. Arizona Snowcap 1.jpg|thumb|''M. vetula'' subsp. ''gracilis'' cv. Arizona Snowcap is one of the popular cultivars.]]
''Mammillaria vetula'' comprises both the least common mammillaria in cultivation and the most common one. Sometime after the 1970s or 1980s, the [[type subspecies]], ''M. vetula'' subsp. ''vetula'', fell out of popularity. The cacti nurseryman John Pilbeam speculates that, because of its plain spination and inconspicuous flowers, it was replaced by showier species. Plants grown in full sun develop the best spination and produce the best blooms, and Pilbeam considers such plants to be "a worthy addition to any collection".<ref name="Pilbeam"/> Pilbeam estimates that, because it breaks up into propagable pieces at the slightest touch and poses no problems in cultivation, ''M. vetula'' subsp. ''gracilis'' is "probably the most commonly grown" mammillaria.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> He notes that it is commonly offered at plant sale events, "except paradoxically at cactus-oriented events, where it would be ignominious to offer it".<ref name="Pilbeam">{{cite book | last=Pilbeam | first=John | title=Mammillaria | publisher=Cirio Publishing Services | series=Cactus file handbook | year=1999 | isbn=978-0-9528302-8-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-hBFAAAAYAAJ | access-date=17 January 2025 | pages=297–298}}</ref>

''Mammillaria vetula'' are tough plants, but require good drainage and do best in sandy soil left to dry out between waterings. Plants require a winter rest in a cold location, without watering, to encourage springtime blooming. It may be grown as a [[houseplant]], in [[rock garden]]s, or in [[xeriscape]]s.<ref name="Extension"/> Cultivars include 'Oruga Blanca', 'Roi Baudouin I', and 'Snow Cap'.<ref name="x156">{{cite book | last=Gómez Sánchez | first=Antonio | title=Enciclopedia ilustrada de los cactus y otras suculentas: descripción de las especies, hábitat y cuidados de cultivo|volume= II | publisher=Floramedia | year=2006 | isbn=978-84-89347-55-7 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TRoqvOo8WFsC&pg=PA83 | language=es | access-date=20 January 2025 | page=83}}</ref>
